title: Xabi Alonso brings real promise but one glaring problem could jeopardise his Chelsea rebuild
description: Alonso could be nurturing one of the most dangerous attacks in the league but has a long-standing problem to solve at the other end of the pitch
fullText:
Xabi Alonso came to Craven Cottage hoping for another Premier League first. Twenty-two years earlier, he bagged his first English top-flight goal for Liverpool. Against a former Reds team-mate striving for the same goal in Alvaro Arbeloa, he made another happy memory on his managerial bow.

Most pictured his return to England to come with Liverpool; Chelsea fans already seem grateful he's landed in London. While far from the perfect performance, victory in a five-goal thriller against Fulham brought a lot of encouragement.

A mixture of big spending and summer snubs seems to have forged one of the most dangerous attacking front threes in the league. Morgan Rogers showed signs he was worthy of his £117m price tag. Cole Palmer, with a point to prove after his World Cup omission, suddenly looked like a real problem again after what was, by his standards, a dud of a season. His link-up with Joao Pedro took effect within 31 seconds.

"They are going to be a very important part of the team," recognised Alonso, who now wants the trio's team-mates to reach the level they exhibited on Monday night. "To build [the team] around them, no. To build the team with them. They need to take responsibility, they need to lead the rest, they need to inspire the rest, because if they do great, the other ones will follow.

"We need to reach them in the best possible situations. We need to have good links to reach them, and they need to help the team to be solid. I'm happy for the three of them. They have played for the team and they have scored, so it's always important for the strikers."

Some Chelsea players are closer to said level than others. Maxence Lacroix was another debutant to impress; his unlikely assist for Rogers was the icing on the cake of a commanding performance in an otherwise imperfect back three. Jorrel Hato was also influential at left wing-back, his attacking impetus showing just how versatile the defender can be in an Alonso system.

There were question marks in the centre of the park, but that was with neither Enzo Fernandez and Moises Caicedo starting. Alonso was pleased by the sound of Chelsea fans singing the Argentinian's name again, even if it was drowned out by deafening boos from the home faithful still bearing a World Cup grudge. "Football is emotional, we have to accept in this situation," said Alonso, keen to move forward with Fernandez in the fold. He now looks likely to stay put this term barring more late transfer drama, while only injury will prevent Caicedo from marshalling Chelsea's midfield, as it did at the Cottage.

But there remains one glaring issue that continues to plague Chelsea, from manager to manager, system to system. Alonso's Premier League return was nearly not so fruitful due to the body between the sticks.

It was another nightmare display from Robert Sanchez, whose trademark howlers put points at risk. Josh King's equaliser, which Sanchez bafflingly let through at his near post, had an xG of 0.07 - the lowest of any goal scored this weekend. He then let the hosts back into the game by parrying Timothy Castagne's strike straight out to Gonzalo Garcia.

For all the club's spending, Sanchez remains the problem player, immune to being usurped from the team by a clear-cut replacement. Maybe 21-year-old Mike Penders will provide the goalkeeping solution long craved, though flinging him straight into the team would go against the club's much-needed move away from the chaos of youth; it didn't work with Filip Jorgensen last year.

Alonso did not seem ready to immediately lose faith in Sanchez as his No 1 after one bad showing. "It's about the team, it's not about the individual. As I said before, we can adjust a few things. The first goal, we can do better to defend, we can do better to avoid, but it's part of the game. We need to accept and to learn from them, and this is going to be a process ... Relax and carry on."

Patience is required for Alonso's rebuild. The belief that he must turn last season's 10th-place team into a title challenger within this season is unfairly ambitious, even if it might be an attitude within the walls of the Stamford Bridge boardroom. Hence there shouldn't be an overreaction when players underperform in the early days of said "process". Levi Colwill and Romeo Lavia, a duo whose progress has been disrupted heavily by injury, were two others who left a lot to be desired against Fulham.

But with Sanchez, entering his fourth season as first-choice stopper, patience is wearing thin. Chelsea got away unscathed this time, but what about next?

Unlike all previous Chelsea managers under the BlueCo regime, Alonso will have an active say on whether this latest Sanchez horror show sparks late action in the transfer window. Emi Martinez is an obvious and available option, if that decision was made.

However, the manager's comments and calm demeanour suggest he'll be against any rash change in personnel at this stage. That may turn out to hamper his project in its all important first year.

title: UK to use Ukraine battlefield data to train AI to protect sensitive sites
description:
London and Kyiv in deal to help stop protesters and hostile states targeting military bases and critical infrastructure
AI models trained on Ukrainian battlefield data will be used to stop protesters and foreign states targeting UK defence sites, railways and energy plants under a deal struck between London and Kyiv.
Private companies will also be given access to the vast trove of data from Ukraine’s Avengers AI lab to help build new systems, the first agreement of its kind in the UK.
 Continue reading...
fullText:
London and Kyiv in deal to help stop protesters and hostile states targeting military bases and critical infrastructure

AI models trained on Ukrainian battlefield data will be used to stop protesters and foreign states targeting UK defence sites, railways and energy plants under a deal struck between London and Kyiv.

Private companies will also be given access to the vast trove of data from Ukraine’s Avengers AI lab to help build new systems, the first agreement of its kind in the UK.

The scheme will be piloted at a UK defence site, building a model to identify protesters or a hostile-state attack. It uses AI-optimised sensors in buried fibre-optic cables to detect different kinds of movement.

The government has suggested the technology, if proven workable, could be used at airports, prisons, railways and energy infrastructure.

The controversial proscription of the activist group Palestine Action was sparked after the group breached RAF Brize Norton on scooters last June, a highly embarrassing security lapse as a result of which the group was able to deface two military aircraft with spray paint before escaping the site without being detained.

Palestine Action said at the time that it had targeted RAF Voyager aircraft used for transport and refuelling, and that “activists have interrupted Britain’s direct participation in the commission of genocide and war crimes across the Middle East”.

Private companies will be able to access the data once approved by the MoD on a secure platform, though the data sharing is likely to raise alarm among privacy campaigners.

Pilot projects have already been approved with three British AI companies – Sintela, Mind Foundry and Skyral. Sintela, a Bristol-based company that specialises in fibre-optic sensors, recently struck a $35m (£26m) deal with the Trump administration to provide surveillance on the US-Mexico border.

The partnership with the Ukrainian AI lab means new UK security systems can be trained on operational drone datasets, strike mission footage and flight profiles, likely to include Russian sabotage attempts against critical Ukrainian infrastructure.

The cache of four years’ worth of military data contains a far deeper picture than models outside Ukraine have previously been trained on, which had been mostly restricted to open-source data.

The government eventually hopes to use the AI models to predict quickly when infrastructure such as railways, the power grid or military bases might be coming under threat or stress from hostile actors.

That would primarily come from the laying of fibre-optic cables that are able to identify unique movements of people or vehicles around sensitive sites. Ministry of Defence sources said that would specifically include when a site might be targeted by protesters – not just hostile states.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said it would be an opportunity for British companies to combine their AI expertise with Ukraine’s battlefield data, which would “accelerate the development of capabilities that not only strengthen our national security but better protect our critical infrastructure and growth in every postcode here at home”.

Other potential projects could include new AI chips to power drones, robotics and automated weapons systems.

Steven Murdoch, a professor of computer science at University College London, said technologies to detect movement from sensors in fibre-optic cables had been around for decades and that it was unclear if data from Ukraine would refine their capabilities.

“I haven’t heard anything that is very convincing, but there is a plausible scenario where they could see something that could be predicted easily and isn’t in any publicly known dataset,” he said.

Ukraine, however, has a lot of other data that may be valuable, especially related to new threats that countries in western Europe might face in the short to medium term.

“What’s valuable is something we’re seeing today which other countries will be worrying about in the future,” Murdoch said. “Anything to do with drones, for example.”

The defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said Ukraine was “pushing the frontier of defence innovation as they bravely resist Putin’s illegal invasion”.

“By combining the UK’s world-leading scientists, engineers and tech companies with Ukraine’s unique battlefield experience and data, we will strengthen both of our nations’ defence and security,” he said.

title: National Police Union Blasts Flock CEO for Turning Against Police
description: The company that built its business on law enforcement trust just lost the largest institution that provided it.
fullText:
Privacy critics have long used Flock's name as their preferred expletive. Now the president of the country's largest police union has sent a similar message to Flock CEO Garrett Langley: a press release titled "Who the Flock Do You Think You Are?"

Fraternal Order of Police National President Patrick Yoes published the statement days after IPVM exclusively documented Langley's turn against his own police customers. The FOP, representing 382,000+ officers, quoted Langley's own prediction that officers would be arrested for abusing Flock, declaring it a breach of the trust the profession had placed in his company.

The FOP statement is the institutional confirmation of a rupture IPVM documented first: one Langley brought on himself. The accountability changes he announced were defensible. Mandatory safeguards, reduced data retention, automatic lockouts for abuse: a company can implement all of that while expressing support for the profession using its product. Langley chose instead to tour ten national outlets predicting mass officer arrests, demoting police from customers to bill-payers, and framing Flock as the institution finally holding law enforcement accountable. None of that was required. It was a choice. The FOP's rebuke is a direct consequence of it. The deeper problem is the pattern it reveals: when Flock faces criticism, Langley finds someone else to blame.

Yoes's central charge, directed at Langley personally, captures the contradiction at the core of Flock's August: a company cannot build a business on police trust and then declare those same officers the problem when public criticism of its product follows. The FOP statement started by quoting Langley's own Vanity Fair prediction back at him:

Yoes did not leave the reversal implicit. He reached back to April, when in Yoes' words, Langley "argued that society already entrusts police officers with enormous responsibilities, including the authority to use force, and questioned why those same officers should not be trusted with license plate reader technology." Those four months had not been quiet ones for Flock: the company was already embattled, in part because Langley had called privacy advocates "terroristic" and accused opponents of wanting to "normalize lawlessness", statements that generated their own backlash and drew national scrutiny. The response to that pressure was not to lower the temperature. It was to open a second front, pinning the blame on the law enforcement community that had defended him by touring ten national outlets to predict mass officer arrests.

The FOP also cited Langley's concession on a specific platform safeguard: "We got this one wrong. We should make it a requirement." That line was not an admission that Langley misjudged his turn against law enforcement. It was an acknowledgment of a technical shortcoming in Flock's product, that a particular safeguard should have been mandatory from the start. The FOP's point was different: that Flock itself has acknowledged failures in its own product, and the response to those failures should be fixing them, not redirecting blame onto officers.

Yoes closed with a call for mutual accountability:

IPVM was the first, and to our knowledge the only, publication to document and analyze Langley's turn against law enforcement as a deliberate strategic shift. Our August 17 report aggregated Langley's statements across 10 interviews, showing a CEO who had repositioned law enforcement from partners to liabilities: demoting police as customers, dismissing the profession as biased and understaffed, and blaming officers for abuse that his own platform fostered. The FOP's August 21 statement responds directly to those same public statements, confirming what IPVM assessed as a fundamental rupture.

Police Support Was Existential to Flock

Flock's relationship with law enforcement was never purely commercial. Officers were advocates: they defended Flock at city councils, pushed back against privacy critics, and helped the company win sole-source contracts that competitors could not touch. Law enforcement veterans like Jamie Hudson, Flock's former Director of Product Consulting and Training, who departed Flock earlier in August 2026 without endorsing its mission on the way out, were hired specifically to translate that trust into institutional relationships. That function is now compromised.

Every accountability change Langley announced was defensible on the merits. Mandatory case codes, automatic lockouts for abnormal search behavior, reduced data retention from 30 days to seven: these are policies a company can implement, and defend, without declaring war on the profession using its product. There is a standard playbook for exactly this situation. Acknowledge isolated misuse. Emphasize that it is rare. Express support for the overwhelming majority of officers who use the system legitimately. Announce the new safeguards as a partnership with law enforcement, not a verdict against it. Companies navigate "bad apples" problems without burning the orchard every day.

Langley chose differently. Across ten national outlets: CNN, Bloomberg, Vanity Fair, Pirate Wires, Puck, SFGATE, TBPN, CBS News, Newsweek, and the Washington Post: he delivered a systematic indictment of law enforcement: calling officers abusers, predicting their mass arrest, calling on state regulators to criminally prosecute his own customers, and declaring to a national television audience that police "might pay the bills" but the community is Flock's real customer. He also described on camera, step by step, exactly how an officer would use Flock to stalk someone. None of those statements were required by any product update he made. They were a choice.

The FOP's rebuke is, in part, a consequence of that choice. Had Langley announced identical policy changes while maintaining the posture of a law enforcement partner, it is unlikely the country's largest police organization would have responded with a press release calling him out by name. The accountability measures were not the provocation. The ten-outlet media campaign portraying police as the threat Flock was built to contain was.

The FOP is not a neutral actor here. Its institutional interest is in protecting officers from accountability, including those who genuinely abused Flock. The documented cases of officers using the platform to track ex-partners across multiple days are real. The FOP's own statement concedes as much: "When an officer intentionally misuses technology, it should be addressed." Langley was addressing it. Readers who are skeptical of law enforcement will read the FOP's statement as exactly what it looks like: the police union protecting officers from consequences for genuine misconduct.

That reading has force. Where it falls short is on the business question. The FOP's objection is not that Flock should ignore abuse. It is that Langley announced his accountability push through a sustained national media campaign that cast the entire law enforcement profession as the threat. A CEO who wants to catch bad cops does not need to appear on ten national outlets predicting mass officer arrests. He needs a working abuse-detection system and a clear policy. Langley built the policy. He also built the media campaign, and those were two distinct choices.

The False Alert Problem Compounds It

Flock's mandatory AI abuse-detection system, Audit Assistance, is already generating false positives on legitimate police searches before its mandatory rollout is even complete. Well-connected law enforcement sources report officers conducting routine, authorized queries being flagged a dozen or twenty times per day. The system has no stated access to case files, dispatch logs, or shift assignments that would distinguish routine patrol from stalking; it infers intent from behavioral patterns alone.

In an ordinary vendor relationship, a wrongly flagged search triggers an administrative review, gets cleared, and the officer moves on. Under Langley's current public posture, the stakes are different. A CEO who has publicly declared he wants officers arrested and fired has made every false positive into a reputational event. An officer wrongly flagged has no visibility into the AI's criteria, no stated appeal mechanism, and a CEO on record predicting their arrest. The technical problem lands on top of the relational one.

Langley's pattern across 2026 is consistent: when Flock faces criticism, he finds someone else to hold responsible. Privacy advocates who raised concerns about his cameras were a "terroristic organization" trying to "normalize lawlessness." Officers who abused his platform became the systemic threat Flock was built to expose. Each pivot reframes his product's failures as someone else's character problem. The FOP's statement is the institutional response to that pattern, from the constituency that had been most loyal to him. Law enforcement defended Flock at city councils, pushed back against privacy critics, and helped him win contracts no competitor could touch. Langley repaid that loyalty by cheering their mass arrest on national television. Whether he can recalibrate his posture toward police before the damage to the company becomes permanent is the question the FOP's statement has forced into the open.

title: Silence Is a Feature
description: The server room is too loud. You picture blue LEDs blinking in the dark. It’s actually a wall of sound - thousands of small fans screaming in slightly different keys, a noise that gets into your teeth. I had the yellow ear protection on and could still feel it in my jaw. Aaron didn’t seem to notice.
fullText:
The server room is too loud. You picture blue LEDs blinking in the dark. It’s actually a wall of sound - thousands of small fans screaming in slightly different keys, a noise that gets into your teeth. I had the yellow ear protection on and could still feel it in my jaw. Aaron didn’t seem to notice. Or he noticed years ago and made his peace.

He walked the row, found the machine, pressed the release. The drive slid out. He held it up, turned it once in the light, and pointed at it with his chin. Grab this.

He seated the new one, waited for the light to go from amber to green, and that was it. Upstairs, a lab full of people kept working on data that had never stopped being there. Not one of them looked up.

Past the double doors, when the noise dropped away and my ears were still ringing, he said: “Silence is a feature.”

I said something. Something like sure.

“No, it’s a feature. Somebody pays for it. You pay, I pay, everybody pays. It’s just not free.” He tapped the dead drive in my hand. “This is the bill.”

“Think about it. No alert. No status page. No email from IT. That’s the product. That big boring nothing, that’s what all the money buys. And when it breaks, the first thing you lose is the quiet. Then somebody walks back in there.” He tipped his head toward the doors behind us.

“Everybody loves builders. But what you actually depend on, every single minute, is maintainers. Water at the pressure you expect. Power that doesn’t flicker. Cables under the ocean. Some kid patching an old library at 2 AM so a bank doesn’t fall over. Somebody is awake right now so all of it feels like nothing to you.”

He dropped the dead drive in a bin by the door with a dozen others just like it. He had a ticket to close and lunch to get.

title: CookWing, an AI chef that doesn't hallucinate quantities
description: AI recipes grounded in real cooking references for more reliable quantities.
fullText:
Ever followed an AI-generated recipe exactly, only to wonder halfway through why it called for 800 g of cheese for four people?

CookWing was built to solve that problem.

AI is great at creating ideas, substitutions, and variations, but it can also make up proportions that simply don’t work. Before Wing builds your recipe, it looks for a real reference recipe from the dish’s culinary tradition and uses it to anchor the ingredient quantities.

Ask for lasagna? The quantities are grounded in an Italian reference recipe. Japanese curry? Japanese references. Korean jjigae, French gratin, Thai curry; the same principle applies.

Wing can still adapt everything to your serving size, available ingredients, allergies, preferences, and cooking style. It just doesn’t invent every quantity from scratch.

The flexibility of an AI chef, grounded in real cooking.

AI FLEXIBILITY, GROUNDED QUANTITIES

• Each generated recipe starts from a real culinary reference.

• Ingredient proportions are anchored before the recipe is personalized.

• Change the servings, ingredients, or dietary requirements while keeping a reliable culinary foundation.

CUSTOM AI RECIPES IN SECONDS

• Describe what you’re craving, the ingredients you have, or what’s left in your fridge. Wing creates a personalized recipe with an image, timings, quantities, and clear instructions.

• Choose the number of servings and your preferred style: quick for busy weeknights, traditional, or restaurant-worthy for a special dinner.

• Add your allergies, food preferences, and pantry staples once. CookWing remembers them for future recipes.

GUIDED COOKING AND BUILT-IN TIMERS

• Follow one clear instruction at a time in a step-by-step cooking mode designed for flour-covered hands.

• Start each step’s timer with a tap. Get an alert right on time, even when your phone is locked.

• Need to change course? Ask Wing while you cook: swap an ingredient, save a sauce, or adjust the cooking time.

MAKE EVERY RECIPE YOUR OWN

• Scale the number of servings in a tap and every ingredient quantity updates automatically.

• Adapt any recipe to make it vegetarian, gluten-free, dairy-free, quicker, or lighter.

IMPORT RECIPES FROM YOUTUBE AND TIKTOK

• Paste a link to a YouTube video or Short, or a TikTok video. CookWing turns it into a complete recipe with ingredients and step-by-step instructions, ready to cook.

GROCERY LIST AND PERSONAL COOKBOOK

• Add recipe ingredients to your grocery list in one tap.

• Save your favorites, find meals you’ve already cooked, and add photos of your finished dishes.

FRESH INSPIRATION EVERY DAY

• Explore new meal ideas in photos every day, from easy weeknight dinners and desserts to dishes from around the world.

Whether you need a quick dinner idea, an easy recipe for beginners, a meal for friends, or a chef-level challenge, CookWing gives you the creativity of AI with quantities grounded in real recipes.

title: Shazam.el
description: Continuing my explorations on malleable computing with Emacs is examining access to OS/Platform-specific resources, in this case with macOS. macOS provides a number of mechanisms for...
fullText:
Continuing my explorations on malleable computing with Emacs is examining access to OS/Platform-specific resources, in this case with macOS. macOS provides a number of mechanisms for high-level inter-process communication, among them AppleScript & Automator Actions (now considered legacy but still maintained) and App Intents, Entities & Shortcuts (introduced in macOS 13 and considered by Apple a replacement for the former).

This post both announces and covers the implementation of an Emacs integration with the Shazam music recognition service that is packaged with macOS. This Emacs integration is called shazam.el (https://github.com/kickingvegas/shazam) and is now available for installation via MELPA.

To understand the shazam.el implementation, the following background information is provided.

Shazam is a music recognition service that is implemented across Apple's different platforms (macOS, iOS/iPadOS, watchOS, tvOS). This service provides a shortcut action (Recognize Music) which is implemented using the following APIs:

App Intent: An expression of an app’s capabilities to the system (in this case the ecosystem of Cocoa-based applications), and contains code to perform that action (App intents | Apple Developer Documentation).

App Entity: Information provided to the system about your app’s data, or about concepts related to your app’s data (App entities | Apple Developer Documentation).

App Shortcut: A workflow (including UI) for orchestrating App Intents and Entities (App Shortcuts | Apple Developer Documentation). There are a number of ways to access a Shortcut, among them via the Shortcuts app or Siri.

With the Recognize Music shortcut action we can realize the Elisp package shazam.el.

A Shortcut (aka workflow) defined in the Shortcuts app can be invoked via command line as follows:

where “shortcut name” is the name given to a Shortcut enclosed by double-quotes.

If the Shortcut is intended to write to stdout, then the shortcuts command line utility must be run into a pipe.

The above incantation lets Emacs run a Shortcut.

The Shortcut used by shazam.el invokes the Recognize Music action and does some work to transform the Shazam search result into a JSON dictionary. The JSON dictionary is written to stdout (iCloud Shortcut: “Identify Music JSON”) which can be read by Emacs and processed.

The sequence diagram below shows the overall integration workflow between Emacs and Shortcuts for shazam.el.

Details on all the features provided by shazam.el can be found in its User Guide. Of note is that once the Shazam search result is deserialized, its content can be processed into a variety of formats. shazam.el takes advantage of this by storing recognized search results into an Org file, using Org markup and properties to store metadata provided by each result. Users can subsequently peruse this history file at their convenience.

This work builds off the explorations in malleable computing with Emacs described in my prior posts:

There is not a lot of Elisp to shazam.el as shown in the cloc result for it:

Most of the challenge in building shazam.el was understanding how start-process worked to asynchronously run the shortcuts command line utility.

A downside to using a Shortcut (workflow) is the requirement to use a binary code-signed representation that is accessed via the Shortcuts app. This makes it less flexible than AppleScript where declaring behavior can be done in plain text. For example, the now-playing.el package can remote-control the Music app via AppleScript that is directly invoked from Emacs built with support for ns-do-applescript. In contrast, accessing contemporary macOS app behavior that is exposed via Intents and Entities requires installing (or creating) a binary code-signed representation (the Shortcut). This adds an extra step (or steps for installing multiple shortcuts) to build an integration with Emacs or any other orchestration tool.

title: Campaigning for cancer screening should not be down to me - Hoy
description: The cycling legend tells BBC Scotland that the onus to encourage men to get tested for prostate cancer should not just be on high profile individuals like him.
fullText:
Sir Chris Hoy believes the onus to encourage men to get tested for prostate cancer should not just be on high-profile individuals like him.

Hoy told BBC Scotland he felt privileged to have the public platform to spread awareness and would continue to do so even if there was a national screening system in place.

But he said: "It shouldn't just be down to high-profile individuals like Jeremy Clarkson or myself or any number of men who've been in a similar situation.

"There should be a more systematic and proactive approach to let men know about their own risk."

Sir Chris was diagnosed with stage 4 prostate cancer when was 47. He turned 50 in March.

He told BBC Scotland: "I turned 50 recently and I got a letter through the post with a bowel screening test.

"I understand the PSA test (a blood test that can help detect prostate cancer) isn't perfect, you know you can get results - not false positives, but it can be that men can be treated when they maybe didn't need to be treated.

"But actually, I think that's not a diagnosis issue, that's a treatment issue, that's a decision for the doctors to make.

"I think knowing your situation is really important."

Hoy said 10,000 men a year in the UK find out too late that they have prostate cancer.

He said there should be some kind of formal process to at least make men take responsibility and ownership and to understand their personal risk.

"In the short term, until something more proactive happens you've got to take it on your own shoulders," he said.

"It's not what you want to think about and it's always the thing you push down the list of priorities. You forget about it because life's busy."

The six-time Olympic gold medallist, was speaking ahead of his "'Tour De 4" charity cycle, the event he founded after his diagnosis which, in his view, is "doing something positive from a very difficult situation."

"The aim is to try and change perceptions of what living with stage 4 cancer can mean," he said.

As well as raising money, he said the event aimed to "bring together people who are in a similar situation to me, to bring together families, people who are remembering loved ones".

"It's really a celebration of life," he said.

While Sir Chris is an ardent campaigner for prostate cancer, he admits to being "moved" by Scottish swimmer Archie Goodburn's impassioned plea to the prime minister for increased funding for brain cancer, and hopes something will come of it.

"So far, it seems that the powers-that-be are listening," he said.

"My concern is that you get a lot of publicity from something like that and then the politicians, or the people in power or whoever the decision-makers are, will do something as a reaction - 'oh yes we're going to have a chat' or 'we're going to do this', but actions speak louder than words.

"You want to see some practical change that will actually be implemented, not just a sit-down-and-talk and 'we might address this' and 'we'll have a look at it' because often that means 'we're just going to kick the can down the road' and nothing actually changes."

"But Archie's not going to give up and I'm not going to give up."

Sir Chris said he was "doing really well" at the moment.

He added: "Right now life just goes on. You could spent your time sitting worrying about the future but that doesn't help you in any shape or form."

The Tour De 4 takes place on Sunday 6 September, starting and finishing at the Sir Chris Hoy velodrome in Glasgow.

title: The Olympic champion re-building her body in a bid for LA 2028
description: Imogen Grant's event, lightweight rowing has been removed from the Olympic calendar. Instead of making weight, now she has to gain it to compete.
fullText:
When British rower Imogen Grant won Olympic gold in Paris, it could easily have been the final race of her career.

Lightweight rowing, the discipline in which she had enjoyed her greatest success, was disappearing from the Olympic calendar. Within days she was back at work as a doctor.

For a while, retirement felt a genuine possibility.

But once her race was over, Grant had a chance to experience the rest of the Paris Games, and something shifted.

"It's so special. I just have to try and do it again," she remembers thinking.

To get to Los Angeles 2028 though, the 5ft 6in rower would have to become a different kind of athlete - and move into open-weight rowing.

There she would have to find a way to compete with women who are usually at least four inches taller and 20kg heavier - an important advantage in a sport where greater size can translate into more power.

Rather than making weight, Grant now needed to gain it.

And she would be doing it on a vegan diet.

For much of Grant's elite rowing career, the scales were an unavoidable part of the job.

To compete in the lightweight women's double sculls, she and partner Emily Craig, who retired last year, had to average no more than 57kg at their pre-race weigh-in.

Open-weight rowing comes with no such restriction.

But she is significantly smaller than many of the women she is now competing with as she targets a place in Britain's quadruple sculls for LA.

"It was definitely a bit daunting thinking about just like physically whether I'd be competitive," the 30-year-old told BBC Sport.

"I'm never going to be the strongest person in the boat."

What Grant does have is the technique and efficiency honed during years of being one of the world's best lightweight rowers.

"It's not just about the raw power in a rowing boat," she explains.

"It's about all of those other things, how well you can row with each other, how well you can move the boat."

The challenge now is to see how much bigger and stronger she can become. That has meant fundamentally changing her relationship with food.

"As a lightweight rower, a lot of the fuelling was really focused on making sure that you were fuelling well for the sessions, but also making sure that you were targeting a specific weight," she adds.

"Now, I don't have that restriction."

The transformation has been gradual.

"I'm heavier now, I'm bigger now, I'm stronger now and I think all of those things are really positive," Grant says.

There is another element to Grant's challenge.

She is vegan - a decision linked to her commitment to climate activism and environmental sustainability. Grant is trying to add muscle while also meeting the huge energy demands of an Olympic endurance athlete.

"We do so much training and eat so frequently that as long as we're getting three good meals a day, what we're eating around the sides, that doesn't really matter so long as it's energy dense," she explains.

"We're an endurance sport, so carbs are king."

Grant estimates that she consumes around 3,500-4,000 calories a day when she's training, significantly more than when she was in lightweight rowing.

The average woman needs 2,000 calories a day.

Protein comes largely through tofu, chickpeas, beans and vegan protein shakes.

Grant is wary of presenting her diet as something remarkable, or suggesting sporting performance alone will persuade others to eat differently.

"I never want it to be a really big part of kind of how I perform, because I don't think that's really how you convince people that being plant-based or reducing meat and dairy is the way to go forward," she says.

"But just consistently showing up and showing that it is possible is really important to me."

Results are beginning to show on the water.

Grant spent much of the period after Paris balancing rowing with her work as a resident doctor in the NHS.

At the 2025 World Rowing Championships in Shanghai she travelled as a reserve.

This year, after returning to full-time rowing, she is in the boat.

In June, she helped Britain's women's quad team win World Cup gold Lucerne.

"It's been going well," she says.

"I think it was a slow and steady start, trying to understand how to fuel and how to gain a bit of weight and gain a bit of muscle.

"I feel like the momentum has been really building."

She has now been selected alongside Paris Olympic champions Lola Anderson and Hannah Scott, plus Finnola Stratton, for this month's World Championships, taking place from 24-30 August in Amsterdam.

"It's such a privilege to race as a lightweight and then turn my hand to seeing if I can throw my lot in with all of the open weight girls, who are so inspiring, and feel that I've got a shot," she adds.

Grant knows there are no guarantees. Reaching Los Angeles, for her, would mark 10 years of representing Britain.

But it is the wider message that appeals to her, as much as the prospect of another Olympics appearance.

"A lot of people think they're not built for rowing because they're too short or too small," she says.

"Showing that that's actually not the case and you can still achieve if you're a little bit smaller is also really important."

"It would just be amazing" she says with a smile.

title: Open-Weight Masked Introspection: Measuring What LMs Can Report About Their Own
description:
Are frontier models able to introspect about their internal states? Recent work suggests that under certain conditions a complex enough model can audit its own internals, call out what changed, and report back confidently about it. We tested that claim on eight open-weight models from seven families and found no such ability: asked whether their own computation had been altered, none answered better than chance. To test it we built Open-Weight Masked Introspection (OWMI), a framework that intervenes on residual-stream sites, attention heads and sparse-autoencoder features, then interrogates the model about the change against the null conditions an answer has to beat: sham runs where nothing was altered, impact-matched random perturbations, and a text-only observer that sees only the visible output.
  Over 78,000 measurements, no model's report discriminates a real intervention from a sham beyond chance (AUROC ~0.

title: 'Don't ask me to print your ChatGPT birthday card': Hitting back at AI 'slop'
description: As artificial intelligence becomes part of our everyday lives, there are some railing against cheaply produced material they say is empty and puts real artists' jobs at risk.
fullText:
When they first started appearing, it was hard to tell where they were coming from, these posters, flyers and food menus that all looked like they had rolled off the same industrial printing press.

Belfast was awash with them during Fleadh Cheoil na hÉireann this month, but by that time most people had them sussed out.

"More AI," they sighed, glancing at a caricatured guitarist on a gig poster or an abnormally glistening burger on a menu.

There were even several images of Ed Sheeran appearing to be making his way around the city.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become part of our everyday lives, and has proven useful for businesses who want to produce promotional material quickly and at little-to-no cost.

But there is a growing backlash from creatives and venue owners, who say 'AI slop' is artistically empty and putting real artists' jobs at risk.

The American Bar in Belfast became one of the first businesses in Northern Ireland to declare itself an AI-free zone, and other bars and restaurants have since ridden in behind.

And the backlash is happening in other places too.

Chris Ferry, who makes greeting cards that specialise in the famous Londonderry sense of humour, doesn't think there is much to joke about when it comes to AI.

In a recent video that attracted thousands of engagements online, he warned customers not to "be coming to me asking me to print a birthday card you've made on ChatGPT ever again".

"It's an insult to me, it's an insult to everybody in the creative industry, and it's an insult to the hard work I've put in here," he said.

Artists of all kinds have reported feeling threatened and cheated by AI.

But Ferry thinks the public don't appreciate that AI-generated imagery risks making graphic designers redundant "the same way AI music disadvantages musicians".

"It's exactly the same but people don't seem to get it," he said.

Recently people have visited his shop and asked him to print designs they created using AI, which he said demonstrates a dissonance around how AI is impacting graphic designers like him.

"I'm very proud and passionate about what I do. I'm a designer, not a print shop, so you come in with a scenario and I'll turn it into a design, and that's why our business works, because we're very different."

Ferry said these instances "really annoyed" him but that he didn't blame the customers.

"It's everywhere, it's convenient, and people just aren't thinking of the repercussions for people like me, so I don't hold it against them.

"The customers who brought in the AI stuff offered to pay but I declined and explained why. It's the principle."

He is "worried about the potential long-term consequences" AI might have on business but he said hopes "the very specific nature of the Derry sense of humour" and "the fact people want stuff made by real people" will future-proof Ferry Clever.

Frances Smyth is a freelance graphic designer who said AI is weighing heavy on her mind too.

When she graduated in 2021 "AI wasn't very present" in her degree.

Now a part-time lecturer at Ulster University and somebody whose job has been affected by the pivot to AI within the creative industry, Smyth said she contemplates the rapidly growing technology a lot.

"Students aren't necessarily encouraged to use it but everybody who is creative has to think about it, because it's so prominent in our industries now."

Many creative agencies, she said, are haemorrhaging clients, as businesses turn to AI for reduce marketing costs.

"As soon as savings is mentioned now, one of the first things businesses think is, 'Could we can use ChatGPT to do that?'

"Often the answer is, 'Yeah, sure'. But the problem is that ChatGPT doesn't do as good a job as an actual artist would. It can't replicate like that authentic artistic expression."

She said AI can be "used for a quick turnaround" but is "regurgitative and soulless".

"Even bad art is better than AI slop. I'd much rather see like a gig poster or a menu done on a post-it note than I would to see it put into ChatGPT.

"Like, I honestly would. It has so much more integrity."

Some venues have recently taken "a principled stance" against the use of AI on their premises, including Mandela Hall, located inside Queen's University Student's Union.

This month, the American Bar in Belfast said it "made the decision to boycott the use of AI" in the pub and on social media.

This included all AI-made artistic material, from music to gig posters.

They said "it constitutes a very real threat to the livelihood of artists" and that the "detriment that AI use has on the environment is well documented".

Speaking to BBC NI, co-owner Tomas Gorman said he believed AI is "a deeply damaging technology, particularly for our local artists and those working in the creative industries".

Co-owner Peter McCloskey added: that "even a shoddily made poster cobbled together by the most inexperienced and computer shy of designers holds within it infinitely more creative value and interesting perspective" than AI.

Like many businesses during the Fleadh, Mal Houston from Three Rivers Restaurant used AI posters to highlight entertainment offerings and food deals.

Then somebody put a sticker on a few of his flyers, reading: "Say no to AI."

"I don't know who had time to do that during the fleadh, but it did make me think."

Houston recently announced that his restaurant and nightclub would no longer be using AI-generated art, "even if it does save a few shillings".

"Hospitality is going through a tough time at the minute, so AI can be convenient and cheap if you need a flyer or menu made up.

"But the other side of that is that it is putting graphic designers out of jobs.

"And just like the hospitality industry is struggling because of challenges we're facing, they're struggling because of AI.

"And that's not fair. These are creative people who've paid to develop their talents at university and because of AI the work just isn't there."

So, while AI remains in its ascendancy and continues to proliferate, a small local - and global - backlash has begun.

And Frances Smyth believes the fight against it is there to be won or lost by each individual.

"People have a sense that the march of AI is inexorable, like we need to embrace it and like it's going to happen anyway.

"But it's not inevitable. Like just I've disabled as much as possible on all my devices and I'm saying no.

"You can do that - say no. We don't need that slop in our lives."

title: The US Navy's next-gen missile breaks cover. It fits inside an F-35 and can threaten enemy aircraft over 280 miles away.
description: The Pentagon is pushing for greater air-to-air reach as China fields increasingly long-range missiles.
fullText:
The US Navy has unveiled a next-generation air-to-air missile.

The AIM-424 "Malice," which is in testing, can threaten enemy aircraft over a range of 280 miles.

Its development comes as the Pentagon pushes for greater air-to-air reach to counter China.

The US Navy has unveiled a new developmental air-to-air missile that can fit inside its F-35 stealth fighter jets and threaten enemy aircraft from over 280 miles away.

Through multiple lines of effort, the Pentagon is pushing for a greater air-to-air reach as China fields increasingly long-range missiles, some of which Pakistan used last year in a brief conflict with India.

The AIM-424 Long Range Air-to-Air Missile (LRAAM), also known as the "Malice," reflects an effort to close the gap. With a stated range of more than 250 nautical miles (288 miles), the munition can travel farther than known alternatives in the Navy's arsenal.

The Navy said in a newly released fact sheet that the Malice is a "next-generation missile intended to strengthen fleet defense and maintain a decisive air domain overmatch against advanced threats." It said the missile is built for fourth-, fifth-, and sixth-generation aircraft.

The Navy published a photo over the weekend showing an AIM-424 missile mounted in the internal weapons bay of the fifth-generation F-35C fighter jet. Storing missiles inside allows the aircraft to maintain its stealth. Services can choose to sacrifice that, though, for a heavier weapons loadout with missiles mounted on the exterior hardpoints.

The Malice is developed by Raytheon, a subsidiary of the US defense contractor RTX. Weighing 1,500 pounds, the weapon is powered by a solid-propellant rocket motor and has a blast-fragmentation warhead, meaning it can damage a target by detonating in proximity.

It's unclear when the Malice will be put into service, but such a reach could prove advantageous for American airpower as the US military looks to counter China in the Western Pacific.

Navy F-35Cs and fourth-generation F/A-18 Super Hornet jets are able to fly with a proven arsenal of air-to-air missiles, including the popular short-range AIM-9 Sidewinder and medium-range AIM-120 AMRAAM, which has been in service for more than three decades.

There's also the AIM-174B Gunslinger, an air-launched version of the SM-6 surface-to-air missile, which is operational on Navy F/A-18 fighter jets. Its range is classified, but it is estimated to be more than 200 miles.

The military is also developing the AIM-260 JATM (Joint Advanced Tactical Missile), designed to compete with Chinese missiles such as the PL-15, which is believed to have a range exceeding 120 miles. The Department of Defense noted the PL-15 and China's other beyond-visual-range air-to-air missiles, such as the newer PL-17, in its latest report on Chinese military capabilities.

It's unclear where the new Malice will fall on the range spectrum, but the stated range is significant. The missile is noticeably larger than the AIM-120; however, it weighs less than the AIM-174B, according to the Navy.

title: Take Five: Six months of war
description: The world's top central bank chiefs gather in Jackson Hole this week against a jittery backdrop, half a year into the Iran war and with bond markets rattled by a selloff in long-
fullText:
Aug 21 (Reuters) - The world's top central bank chiefs gather in Jackson Hole this week against a jittery backdrop, half a year into the Iran war and with bond markets rattled by a selloff in long-dated U.S. debt that prompted U.S. Treasury intervention.

Away from Wyoming, there's plenty else going on, from inflation readings around ‌the world and Nvidia's earnings to a South Korean rate decision and an Icelandic vote on whether to revive EU accession talks.

Here's all you need to know about ‌the week ahead in financial markets, by Howard Schneider in Washington, Laura Matthews in New York, Stine Jacobsen in Copenhagen, Gregor Stuart Hunter in Singapore and Samuel Indyk in London.

Big-think or red meat? That's the choice Fed Chairman ​Kevin Warsh faces as he prepares a keynote address at the Fed's Jackson Hole symposium in Wyoming: expound on his ideas for reforming the central bank, or stick to the nuts and bolts of monetary policy and whether rates are headed higher.

As the gathering kicks off on Thursday, bringing together central bank chiefs from around the world, the audience for his remarks could hardly be more influential.

Warsh has spent his first weeks as chair focusing on long-term structural issues facing the U.S. economy. But investors, still digesting a bond selloff, are craving a steer about the here and now.

Warsh has been pretty clear ‌he doesn't want to show his hand, but he may find his ⁠no-guidance policy becoming a liability.

The prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz and crude prices grinding higher are adding to concerns about the global inflation outlook.

Brent is headed for a second straight weekly gain and its sixth advance in eight weeks, but it's the surge in refined products ⁠that is drawing growing attention as the Northern Hemisphere heads towards the colder months.

European diesel prices have jumped more than 70% since the outbreak of war in February; U.S. gasoline is up 60%. With refining output curtailed in the Middle East, Russia, East Asia and beyond, energy-driven inflation looks here to stay.

A clearer picture of global inflation is due in the coming days, with data from Australia on Wednesday, and France, Spain ​and ​Tokyo on Friday. Particular focus will fall on the U.S. core PCE reading on Wednesday - expected to print above ​the Fed's 2% target for the 65th consecutive month.

After a ‌rocky few days for tech stocks, investors will get a fresh read on the artificial intelligence spending boom that has helped propel markets to record highs when Nvidia reports second-quarter results on Wednesday.

title: A women's shelter for refugees in Poland fights for survival as anti-Ukrainian sentiment rises
description: When Nastya Podorozhnya's relatives fled the war in Ukraine for neighboring Poland, volunteers welcomed them with open arms.  Podorozhnya, 29, was already living in Poland when the war began.  As she ...
fullText:
KRAKOW, Poland (AP) — When Nastya Podorozhnya's relatives fled the war in Ukraine for neighboring Poland, volunteers welcomed them with open arms.

Podorozhnya, 29, was already living in Poland when the war began. But days before Russia's full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, she rushed back to Ukraine to help her sister and nieces get out.

As she returned to Poland alongside an influx of refugees in the war's first days, she witnessed the outpouring of support from Polish volunteers. But she also spotted a risk: Ukrainian women accepting help from strangers could become vulnerable to human traffickers.

That was when she decided to found Martynka, a helpline and support group for female Ukrainian refugees escaping gender-based violence.

Four years later, she is struggling to keep the organization afloat. Funding for refugee support is drying up, hostility toward Ukrainians is growing, and Poland still lacks a long-term integration strategy. As war fatigue deepens, politicians are increasingly exploiting anti-refugee sentiment for political gain.

The shift is being felt by groups such as Martynka. While fundraising was relatively easy in the first months of the war, international donors have since turned their attention to other global crises.

Martynka's shelter, located in an inconspicuous two-bedroom apartment in central Krakow, has hosted more than 100 women and children. Women receive help to escape abusers and access medical care, psychological support, jobs and housing.

"It often starts with me having tea in this very kitchen with the women and they tell me what happened to them and I say 'girl, same,'" Podorozhnya told The Associated Press during an interview in the Krakow shelter, referring to her own experience of a man trying to rape her on a street in Poland in 2016.

As Podorozhnya and her colleagues struggle to raise enough money to keep the shelter open, she says calls for donations frequently trigger a torrent of online abuse.

"It's because I'm Ukrainian," she said.

Around 3.5 million Ukrainians fled to Poland in the first weeks of the war, according to the U.N. Poles greeted them at train stations and opened their homes to them, while the government granted refugees access to jobs and social security benefits.

The two countries share a long history of brutality at the hands of Russia, and Poland remains a key ally to Ukraine in the war.

In addition to the refugees, most of whom are women and children, more than 1 million Ukrainians were already living in Poland before the war, primarily as economic migrants.

The refugees have increasingly become targets of anti-Ukrainian rhetoric. In research published this year, Ukrainian migrants interviewed by Olena Babakova, a researcher at Warsaw's Vistula University, identified the 2025 Polish presidential campaign as the period when anti-Ukrainian feeling intensified, as it became a common theme for all parties, not just the far right.

Karol Nawrocki, representing the national-conservative camp and who eventually won the presidency, promised legislation that would prioritize Polish citizens over Ukrainians when accessing public services. Rafał Trzaskowski, the liberal candidate, proposed restricting child welfare benefits for Ukrainians.

As tensions increased, historical grievances between the countries resurfaced.

In June, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyydecided to name a military unit after a Ukrainian paramilitary organization accused of massacring Poles during World War II, causing outrage in Poland. Nawrocki responded by withdrawing a state honor awarded to Zelenskyy, further escalating the tensions.

"And it's not only negative feelings, Ukrainians really experience hostile conversations and attacks," Babakova told the AP.

According to data from the Polish police, 180 Ukrainian citizens were victims of prejudice-motivated crimes by mid-July, a significant increase compared with 275 for the whole of 2025 and 267 in 2024.

In response to multiple media reports of Ukrainians beaten on Polish streets over the summer, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said in late July that "we must wage war on violence and hatred."

The Polish government has been steadily cutting support for Ukrainian refugees, saying that many have stabilized their situation.

Poland's ombudsman has warned that the changes disproportionately affect the most vulnerable groups, including single mothers with several children, older people and those with chronic illnesses or disabilities. Because most Ukrainian men of military age, between 23 and 60, are prohibited from leaving the country, single mothers are overrepresented among the refugees.

Yuliia Repenko from the Ukrainian House said that her nongovernmental organization, which provides help to Ukrainians, was "increasingly supporting people who are particularly vulnerable to exclusion."

The Polish government has defended its decision to cut back aid to Ukrainian refugees. Katarzyna Nowakowska, Poland's deputy minister for family, labor and social policy, told the AP that the most vulnerable applicants still receive direct help from the state and any other refugees needing support should turn to social workers.

As the Polish government has been scaling back its support, international aid has also declined, further limiting options. Data from the U.N. refugee agency shows a steady drop since 2022 in the funding provided by international donors for Ukrainians, with only half the agency's identified needs financed this year, compared with 94% in 2022.

"Financial supporters have moved on from helping Ukrainian refugees, but the war is still ongoing," said Sonia Novytska, a Martynka helpline worker. "If anything, it has become deadlier since the start."

Martynka received about 1,800 requests for help last year, and staff expect that number to increase, Novytska said. Not only victims of violence contact the helpline now, but also mothers struggling to provide food and shelter for their children.

"What Poles need to understand is that we are helping the people that could otherwise become homeless in their neighborhoods, the people who might start abusing substances out of despair they can't make ends meet," Podorozhnya said.

"Martynka does the job of the Polish state," she said.

title: Police investigating death of Southwest flight attendant on Hawaii layover

fullText:

title: Democrat rips Hasan Piker as 'hack who thrives on hate' over his warning to American Jews about Israel
description: Rep. Hillary Scholten condemned Hasan Piker's remarks about American Jews and Israel, calling the Twitch streamer a "hack who thrives on hate."
fullText:
Controversial far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who has become increasingly prominent in Democratic politics, is facing backlash from Rep. Hillary Scholten, D-Mich., over his remarks about American Jews' support for Israel that she characterized as "talk of violence" targeting Jewish Michigan state Sen. Jeremy Moss.

In a statement published Monday, Scholten said Piker was "a hack who thrives on hate, shock and awe because he lacks substance."

"Hasan Piker's talk of violence against American Jews, and directly naming a Michigan elected official, and future member of Congress, Jeremy Moss, is unacceptable. Full stop," Scholten's statement read. "We should all be calling out this disgusting rhetoric so it loses its grip on our politics once and for all. It has no place in Michigan, and no place in our country."

Hasan Piker Is Becoming The 'Face Of The Progressive Movement,' Former Democratic Operative Warns

In his response to Scholten's statement, Piker called Scholten an "Israel 1st congresswoman."

"if i was an israel 1st congresswoman with a possible cheating scandal with a republican in the state, i wouldn't spend so much time vying for the spotlight by actively defaming a prominent antizionist voice to harm the dem senate majority chances over a 90/10 issue," Piker wrote on X.

Piker, who holds a large social media following, has been particularly visible in Michigan this election cycle. He backed Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who defeated Rep. Haley Stevens in a primary earlier this month. El-Sayed was criticized for appearing with Piker during his campaign, with some saying that the streamer's rhetoric was too extreme.

Scholten backed Stevens last month, calling her a "smart, capable, and common-sense leader." She later praised Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer for endorsing Stevens.

El-Sayed also responded to Piker's comments, and while he did not condemn the streamer outright, he denounced antisemitism and rhetoric that puts the Jewish community in danger.

"I believe all Americans deserve the right to advocate for what they believe without fear of violence. This is particularly true for communities that have been intimidated for their beliefs in the past," El-Sayed wrote.

"My commitment to Jewish safety is the same as my commitment to the safety of my own daughters," he added. "Antisemitism is a scourge, and we need to address it in all its forms. And I stand against any rhetoric that puts the community at risk."

El-sayed Disavows Hasan Piker's 9/11 Comments But Decries 'Cancel Culture'

In his statement, El-Sayed stressed that Piker did not speak for his campaign, writing that, "nobody speaks for this campaign besides me and my campaign spokespeople."

In addition to politicians, Piker was also criticized by Jewish organizations.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, the Jewish Federation of Detroit said that "Hasan Piker's talk of violence against Jewish Americans while displaying a picture of a Michigan lawmaker who is Jewish is repugnant and antisemitic."

"We call on all responsible leaders to condemn this extremist, attention-seeking conduct which divides Americans, foments hate, and makes our Jewish community less safe," the Jewish Federation of Detroit's statement read.

The American Jewish Committee (AJC) also said on Monday that by using an image of Moss, "Piker put a target on the backs of Sen. Moss, Jewish candidates and officeholders, and American Jews alike."

"Blaming Jews for the antisemitism directed at them is itself antisemitism," AJC wrote on X. "Every public official who has shared his platform now has a choice: denounce this and walk away, or be complicit. There is no third option."

Anti-Defamation League CEO Jonathan Greenblatt weighed in as well, questioning whether elected officials who associate with Piker really watch his streams or if "they just see his reach and ignore the rampant antisemitism."

"The Jewsplaining is extraordinary: Piker appoints himself an authority on antisemitism, lecturing Jews about what is and isn't antisemitic while blaming the Jewish community for the hatred directed against it," Greenblatt said of Piker.

Click Here For More Coverage Of Media And Culture

During his Aug. 20 stream, Piker seemed to warn American Jews against supporting Israel, saying that doing so could lead to violence against them.

"People don't f--- with Israel any longer. And if Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they're singularly invested in Israel, eventually someone will come around and take action not against Israel, mind you, but against American Jews," Piker said.

When he made the comment, Piker had an image of Moss, who is running to fill Stevens' seat, in his background.

Piker's remarks came amid a controversy over an audio clip circulating online in which Moss purportedly said that the "entire purpose" of his congressional campaign was to ensure America's continued support for Israel.

However, the Michigan Democrat said that the clip was fabricated, calling it "a manipulated and unsourced audio, with things I never did and never would say."

"We are in a dangerous era of disinformation. Circulating a lie because it affirms your bias or belief is equally bad whether it comes from the left or the right. We all have a choice not to spread fabricated images, videos, and audio about candidates and campaigns. We all have a role in stopping the erosion of our democracy," Moss said about the controversy over the audio clip.

Fox News Digital reached out to Piker and Moss for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

title: Six months into Iran war, almost half of global oil flows from war zones
description: , Anushree Mukherjee and Robert Harvey LONDON Aug 25 (Reuters) - Almost half the world's oil comes from countries affected by conflict in 2026, Reuters calculations show, underscoring
fullText:
LONDON Aug 25 (Reuters) - Almost half the world's oil comes from countries affected by conflict in 2026, Reuters calculations ‌show, underscoring that current disruptions have eclipsed previous energy crises.

Six months ago, U.S. ‌and Israeli attacks on Iran triggered what has become the largest oil supply crisis on record, with no clear ​end in sight.

What countries are driving the global oil crisis?

What impact is refining capacity loss having globally?

How are emergency oil stockpiles being used currently?

How severe is the current oil supply disruption?

At the same time, the Russia-Ukraine war has forced production and refining cuts, including in nearby Kazakhstan this year.

Ongoing conflict in Libya and U.S. restrictions on Venezuelan oil exports at the start of the year have added further strain.

Together, countries affected by those conflicts produced ‌about 45 million barrels per ⁠day of oil based on 2025 output, accounting for more than 43% of global supply, according to Reuters calculations using International Energy Agency data.

The ⁠disruptions have increased the world's reliance on U.S. oil supplies, though that too has occasionally been disrupted by severe weather.

Not all of this year's supply disruptions happened at the same time.

With Saudi Arabia ​re-routing ​oil to the Red Sea and Gulf exporters ​sneaking oil secretly out of the ‌Strait of Hormuz, the current Gulf oil disruption stands at around 5 million to 7 million bpd, according to analysts' estimates.

But risks to total flows remain high, as attacks in the Red Sea and near Egypt's Suez Canal in July demonstrated.

The conflicts in the Gulf and Ukraine have also cut global refining capacity by about a tenth.

Ukraine has targeted much of ‌Russia's refining network, striking plants as far away as ​Omsk, about 2,700 km (1,680 miles) from Ukrainian-held territory.

Russia is ​grappling with fuel shortages and has ​banned gasoline and diesel exports, tightening global fuel markets.

Higher fuel prices have ‌become a key driver of inflation, contributing ​to higher borrowing costs ​and helping to push U.S. debt to a record $40 trillion.

U.S. diesel prices have climbed to record levels despite refiners running at peak capacity.

The IEA has released record volumes ​from emergency stockpiles to ‌help cushion the supply shock. Those releases are now largely complete, even as global ​inventories continue to decline.

title: Lindsay Clancy trial: Postpartum is real, but child killing demands accountability, veteran prosecutor says
description: Veteran child abuse prosecutor Jonathan Hatami says public support for Lindsay Clancy is overshadowing the three children she is accused of killing.
fullText:
If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

While failures by people, medical professionals and systems around Lindsay Clancy deserve scrutiny, nothing should erase a parent's responsibility for killing a child, according to a veteran prosecutor who said he's concerned that public support for the Massachusetts mom is overshadowing the killing of her three young children.

Clancy is accused of killing her three young children — Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months — and trying to end her own life by dropping from a second-floor window after sending her husband to pick up takeout and something from a pharmacy, according to the Plymouth County District Attorney's Office.

But as the case has drawn national attention, Clancy has also attracted supporters both online and in-person at the courthouse, and experts have warned that that support has taken attention away from the victims.

Lindsay Clancy's Three Child Victims Forgotten Amid Crowds Of Support: Mother Of Six

"Nobody who murders children is a victim no matter what they're suffering through," said Jonathan Hatami, a veteran child abuse prosecutor. "You're never a victim if you murder people because victims don't do something. Something happens to them."

The defense does not dispute that Clancy caused the deaths — but she has pleaded not guilty and is contesting criminal responsibility.

Hatami has spearheaded a number of high-profile cases against child abusers in Los Angeles, California, including the murder of 8-year-old Gabriel Fernandez, who was tortured and killed by his mother and her boyfriend. Gabriel's killing exposed a series of missed red flags by the county's Department of Children and Family Services and inspired a Netflix docuseries.

Lindsay Clancy Defense Scores 'Extremely Helpful' Psychosis Concession As Expert Flags Next Hurdle

"Gabriel Fernandez was tortured and murdered by his mom and her boyfriend — however, there were a lot of other people...that were responsible," Hatami told Fox News Digital. "There were a lot of people that missed signs through the eight or nine months of Gabriel's torture. There were a lot of people in government, in law enforcement, social workers, who missed all these different signs that really could have saved Gabriel — and they didn't do it. However, Pearl Fernandez and Isauro Aguirre were ultimately responsible for the torture and murder of Gabriel and were prosecuted for that and they were convicted of that."

Lindsay Clancy Murder Trial Becomes Social Media Obsession As Tiktokers, Sleuths Debate Controversial Case

In Clancy's case, he argued, many of the people and systems around her deserve scrutiny — but that should not turn her into the central victim of the story. In his view, she's been too much of the focus.

"Instead of about the three victims who were innocent kids," he said.

Follow The Fox True Crime Team On X

While failures of government and the child welfare system were investigated after Gabriel's murder, that didn't take responsibility away from the killers, he said. And in the Clancy case, he said he sees a risk that the focus on her mental health could eclipse the three children who were killed in their own home.

"I didn't see people out in the streets cheering on Pearl Fernandez because there were other people that were somewhat responsible for what happened to Gabriel," he said. "And the same thing plays in this case. Lindsay admitted to strangling her three children to death. She admitted to strangling them to death with exercise cords."

Lindsay Clancy Described A Male Voice Ordering Her To 'Kill Her Children And Kill Herself': Testimony

Clancy's defense has said she sought help repeatedly as she struggled with depression, sleeplessness, suicidal thoughts and voices urging her to harm herself and the children.

Like What You're Reading? Click Here For More

Defense attorney Kevin Reddington has argued that Clancy was under the effects of postpartum psychosis, while prosecutors allege she acted deliberately and understood what she was doing was wrong.

"If you murder your children, you need to be held accountable and responsible for that," Hatami said. "No matter what the whys are, no matter what reasons are."

Susan Smith Eligible For Parole Again After Being Denied Release For Drowning Her 2 Sons In 1994

If convicted of any of the three counts of first-degree murder she faces, Clancy would see a sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"Your children should be your life. And if you take their life, you should, as a person, want to be punished for that," Hatami said.

Fox News' Sarah Rumpf-Whitten and Adam Sabes contributed to this report.

Putin ‘panicked’ as defiant Ukraine marks Independence Day under Russian bombardment
description: Ukraine celebrated 35 years of independence amid fresh Russian attacks as an expert said Kyiv’s deep strikes and battlefield pressure have left Putin rattled.
fullText:
Ukraine marked its 35th Independence Day on Monday under the shadow of continued Russian attacks, with one regional security expert arguing that Russian President Vladimir Putin is "panicked" as Ukrainian forces strike deeper inside Russia.

The anniversary, commemorating Ukraine's Aug. 24, 1991, declaration of independence from the Soviet Union, came amid intensified Russian strikes on civilian infrastructure and heightened security concerns after Ukraine's Security Service warned of possible terrorist attacks ahead of the holiday.

European leaders joined Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv for Independence Day events in a show of support as the war grinds on. Zelenskyy declared that Ukraine wants peace but is not prepared to surrender to Moscow's demands.

A Russian drone strike Friday on a packed shopping center in Kryvyi Rih, Zelenskyy's hometown, killed at least 16 people and injured 130, according to The Associated Press.

'Pure Hell' In Moscow As Ukrainian Drones Strike Major Refinery Supplying Capital's Fuel Market

Putin has warned that Ukrainian strikes on Russian economic targets open a "Pandora's box," while Kyiv maintains deep strikes are vital to disrupting Moscow's logistics.

Ukraine has targeted Russian economic infrastructure, including warehouses belonging to online retailers Wildberries and Ozon.

"The war with Russia has seen a lot of advances for the Ukrainians over this year," former Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Carrie Filipetti, now executive director of the Vandenberg Coalition, told Fox News Digital.

"They've recently been able to actually penetrate much deeper into Russian territory, including close to Moscow and St. Petersburg."

"Their success on the military front has now resulted in the Russians getting panicked and starting to attack more inside Ukraine and what they're really trying to do is weaken their will and capabilities," Filipetti said, adding that Putin "gets very anxious when he's put in a corner."

"What we're seeing is these sorts of gasps at trying to retain some kind of control," Filipetti added. "This is why he recently targeted a shopping mall inside Ukrainian territory. He is not focused on targeting military assets. He is really focused on trying to defeat the will of Ukrainians by attacking them."

Russia Unleashes Nearly 600 Missiles And Drones On Kyiv In Deadliest Strike Since May

Filipetti warned the targeting of civilian areas created heightened security risks as Ukraine marked its 35th Independence Day, more than four years into Russia's full-scale invasion.

Several European leaders traveled to Kyiv for Ukraine's Independence Day events, including European Council President António Costa and leaders from Finland, Lithuania, Norway, Denmark, Estonia and Latvia.

Filipetti said the high-level participation underscored continued international support for Ukraine.

Trump's Turkey Arms Sale Proposal Sparks Congressional Questions Before Nato Summit

"Independence Day is a really important moment for the allies of the Ukrainians to really show that we are not losing steam, that we continue to support their operations, to continue to support their sovereignty," Filipetti said. "But anytime there's massive public gatherings, particularly to demonstrate patriotism and support for the Ukrainian state, it increases the security risk."

Ukrainian authorities urged citizens to stay vigilant on public transport and guard against potential sabotage or sharing media that could reveal military positions, as well as possible attacks, Ukrainian News reported.

"They should be particularly mindful about sharing any videos or photographs that could betray the locations of some of their frontline soldiers," Filipetti warned.

Drone Offensive Hits Russian Oil Tankers And Refineries At 'Industrial Scale' As Moscow Bans Diesel Exports

Monday's holiday came after a lethal exchange of drone and missile strikes. Ukrainian officials reported at least seven deaths from Russian attacks, while a Ukrainian drone strike in Russia's Krasnodar region killed three, according to Russian officials, The Associated Press reported.

"The Russians really want to bleed the Ukrainians of people, equipment, and will before the Russians are bled of those same three things," Filipetti said. "And what we've seen over the course of this year is almost no territorial gains on behalf of the Russians."

They are losing more soldiers each month than they can recruit, forcing them to rely on North Korean, Cuban and other foreign fighters to fill the gap, Filipetti added.

Zelenskyy Says Putin 'Lost The Initiative' As Ukraine's Tech Industry Reshapes The War

"Remember, Putin thought that this was going to be a special military operation that was going to last a matter of weeks," Filipetti said.

Ultimately, she emphasized that Ukraine's resolve delivers a firm deterrent beyond Moscow.

"It sends a message to the Russians that any invasion of sovereign territory, like their invasion of Ukraine, is going to create more consequences for them," Filipetti said. "We are not losing steam, and we continue to support their operations, to continue to support their sovereignty."

Filipetti said it also sends an important message to other American adversaries like China.

"These adversaries of the United States really learned from how the United States handles conflicts in other theaters. It's really important that our adversaries of China, Russia, Iran, and others understand that if they invade another country unilaterally, there are going to be consequences, not rewards."
